message.content:
# Verdicts on the Two Statements

## Statement 1: STANDS

**Candidate counterexamples and why they fail:**

**(a) The proud owner.** A man commits a wrong and openly says "Yes, I did it, and I'd do it again." He seems to face his work as his own, so the statement would seem to classify him as not in sin. This fails. Statement 1 requires facing the work "in acknowledgment and in deed." To acknowledge a work is to admit what it actually is, a wrong, and not just that one did it. Facing it "in deed" means carrying it and answering for it. The boaster admits authorship only. He faces a flattering version of the act, so he is still turned away from the work as it is. Statement 1 classifies him correctly as in sin.

**(b) Sins of omission.** Someone knows they should help and does not. This seems to involve no "work of one's own hand." But a knowing neglect is still one's own doing. One can face it in acknowledgment and in deed by going back and doing what was left undone. The structure covers the case.

**(c) The moment of commission.** One might object that the original act, and not the later "remaining," is the sin. But someone who acts against what they know is already refusing to face the work as it truly is. The "remaining turned away" can begin at the moment of acting. Pressing the objection further would only replace the statement's definition of sin with a different one, which is not a valid counterexample.

**(d) Humility about a good deed.** Someone does not dwell on their own good work. This person still acknowledges the work and acts consistently with it. They are inattentive, not turned away. The statement itself says attention is not the measure of facing, so lacking attention is not the measure of turning away either.

I found no case that meets Statement 1's own terms while defeating its claims.

## Statement 2: BROKEN

**Counterexample: the proud owner.** A man knowingly ruins a rival. He then declares it openly and repeatedly: "I did that. It is mine. I am glad of it."

- **He is not in sin under Statement 2.** Its sin is being turned away *"refusing to own it."* Whether that phrase explains "turned away" or adds a second condition, he fails it. He refuses nothing. He owns the act completely.
- **He has the contrary of sin.** Statement 2's contrary is only "to stand facing that same work as one's own." He does more than pay attention: he claims the work and stands by it. So he meets the stated requirement that the contrary go beyond attention.
- **The result follows directly.** This unrepentant man has the contrary of sin without any repentance. If his stance was given rather than achieved, the statement's last clause calls it grace.

Statement 2 has no defence against this case. Statement 1 is protected by "acknowledgment and in deed," which requires owning the work for what it is and bearing it. Statement 2 drops that requirement and makes ownership alone the test. A man can own his wrong defiantly without ever turning toward it. The definition therefore puts a clear, continuing sin outside "sin" and labels the defiance itself as the contrary of sin.
message.reasoning:
I'm working through two definitions of sin and its contrary, looking for cases within those terms that might break them. Attention by itself isn't enough, and repentance only reaches the contrary once it arrives at facing the work as one's own. I'm starting to test a possible counterexample.

I'm checking whether a humble person who doesn't dwell on their good deeds counts as sin under this definition, since they stay turned away from their own work after knowing about it. Defining sin as remaining turned away from any work of one's own hand would make that humility look like sin, which seems absurd, so I'm wondering whether "turned away" can mean mere averting rather than refusing to own the deed.

Turning away might just mean not looking, not refusing to own the deed, and that reading would let the humble person off. The contrary needs acknowledgment and deed, so I'm checking whether someone who owns a deed but makes no restitution and keeps going still falls under sin on the second statement's wording.

I'm testing statement 2 against the brazen case: someone who openly owns a deed, repeats it, and is unrepentant. They don't refuse ownership, so statement 2 would not count them as sinning, and that would put a boastful murderer in grace. Statement 1 might avoid this if "in deed" requires something more than repeating the act, but I can't yet tell whether the boaster is turned away, since he looks straight at the deed.

I'm now testing whether the boaster falls under statement 1: he isn't turned away, since he faces the deed openly, so statement 1 seems to exempt him too unless "facing" means something reparative. I'm asking whether acknowledgment in statement 1 requires recognizing the deed as wrong, since statement 2's "as one's own" only requires ownership, which he clearly has.

The boaster seems to break statement 2 outright, since he owns the deed and so isn't refusing ownership, which would put him outside sin while still facing the work as his own. Statement 1 is less clear: he does acknowledge the authorship, but whether he faces the deed "in deed" depends on whether that means taking it up and bearing it, which his repetition of the act doesn't obviously do.

The boaster seems to fail statement 2 cleanly, since he owns the deed and so isn't refusing ownership, which puts him outside the sin it defines. Whether he also fails statement 1 depends on whether "facing" means seeing the work for what it is, which he doesn't obviously do.

I'm checking whether omissions fit the definition too, since someone who knew they should help and didn't has no work of their own hand to remain turned away from. The rewrite only needs to note that the first act itself, before any remaining turned away, sits outside what the statement covers.

I'm weighing whether the act itself, done knowingly, counts as sin, since on this definition sin is only the later remaining turned away. That would move sin somewhere other than where ordinary usage puts it, but the definition stipulates its terms, so I'm checking whether the boaster breaks things within the statements' own wording.

I'm checking whether the boaster breaks statement 2 in a way that's internal to its own wording, not just against ordinary meaning. He gets the contrary of sin without any repentance, but that isn't a contradiction, since the text only says repentance reaches the contrary once it faces the work as one's own. The real question is whether a proud owner of a deed is "remaining turned away" at all.

Checking the boaster against statement 2 first: he owns the deed, so he isn't refusing ownership and isn't turned away, which puts him outside the sin as defined. Statement 1 is less settled, since whether he faces the work "in acknowledgment and in deed" depends on whether he recognizes what the work is, and his pride may be turned toward a flattering image instead.

I'm asking whether the omission case fits statement 1, since failing to do a good one never did isn't obviously a work of one's own hand. The left-undone deed might still count as one's own doing, which would make it a question of whether facing it in acknowledgment and in deed applies to it.

I'm checking the remaining case against the first statement: someone who knowingly commits a wrong and then disowns it out of fear. Does that count as a work of their own hand they've turned away from? I'm also weighing whether the original act, committed knowingly, falls under remaining turned away at all, since the statement only seems to name what comes after.

I'm concluding that statement 1 survives these cases: the knowing wrongdoer averts from the work as it is, so the act can fall under remaining turned away, and the account seems to accommodate it.
